Some performers are so concerned about completing their set that they treat every song like an item to be checked off: Song one—done. Song two—done. Next. But music is not a shopping list. A vocalist may sing a powerful chorus and immediately rush into the next verse because the rehearsal plan says, “Keep moving.” Sometimes, however, the emotional weight of that chorus deserves a moment. Perhaps the pianist allows the final chord to breathe. The singer repeats one significant line. The band answers with a short musical phrase. The choir sustains the harmony before resolving. That moment may communicate more than another hurried song. Nothing has been added merely for show. The music is simply being allowed to finish its thought. As a voice coach, I teach singers that communication does not happen only through words. Breath, silence, dynamics, tone, phrasing and space also communicate. A singer who is constantly thinking about the next song may never fully inhabit the current one. Romancing the song does not mean dragging it unnecessarily. It means staying with it long enough for its emotional and musical message to arrive. It means recognizing when a musical moment has something more to say—and having the confidence to let it speak. “A song should not be abandoned simply because its written arrangement has ended; sometimes its final meaning needs a moment to breathe.” — Victor Adenola #art #band #bands #choir #churchchoir #creativity #music #musicDirector #musicProducer #musicians #musicperformance #performance #performancetips #singer #singers #singersgospelSingers #songStructure #stagepresence
